lessons.title: Potential Outcomes and the Missing Counterfactual
lessons.summary: Define causal effects as comparisons between outcomes that cannot both be observed.

contentBlocks.text: Potential Outcomes and the Missing Counterfactual

For one unit, the potential outcome under treatment and under control cannot be observed simultaneously. Causal inference replaces that missing counterfactual with design assumptions—randomization, exchangeability, positivity, and consistent treatment definitions—that must be defended rather than hidden behind a model score.
Principal-level reasoning
items: State the intervention and outcome before choosing an estimator.
Separate identification assumptions from statistical estimation.

lessons.title: DAGs and the Backdoor Criterion
lessons.summary: Use directed acyclic graphs to reason about confounding without conditioning on the wrong variables.

contentBlocks.text: DAGs and the Backdoor Criterion

A causal DAG encodes assumed directions among variables. A valid adjustment set blocks non-causal backdoor paths from treatment to outcome without conditioning on descendants of treatment or colliders, which can create bias instead of removing it.
Principal-level reasoning
items: Draw causal assumptions before inspecting coefficient significance.
Test whether a candidate variable is a confounder, mediator, or collider.

contentBlocks.text: More controls are not always safer: conditioning on a collider opens a spurious path.

challenge.explanation: More controls are not always safer: conditioning on a collider opens a spurious path.

contentBlocks.text: Estimate a Difference-in-Means ATE

Under valid random assignment, the average treatment effect can be estimated by the difference between treated and control means. Production code must reject empty arms, expose arm counts, and retain enough statistics for confidence intervals and audit.

Return arm means and counts alongside the effect.

lessons.title: Experimentation Platform Boundaries
lessons.summary: Separate assignment, exposure, outcome, and analysis so causal evidence survives service failures.

contentBlocks.text: Experimentation Platform Boundaries

An experiment platform needs deterministic assignment, immutable experiment configuration, exposure logging at the moment treatment is actually delivered, governed metric definitions, and analysis that joins by stable units. Logging assignment alone overstates exposure when delivery fails.
Principal-level reasoning
items: Randomize at a unit that prevents cross-arm contamination.
Version allocation, eligibility, and metric definitions together.

contentBlocks.text: Causal analysis is only as credible as the path from assignment through actual exposure to outcome.

challenge.explanation: Causal analysis is only as credible as the path from assignment through actual exposure to outcome.
hints: Randomize at a unit that prevents cross-arm contamination.

lessons.title: Interference and Contaminated Units
lessons.summary: Recognize when one unit's treatment changes another unit's outcome.

contentBlocks.text: Interference and Contaminated Units

Standard experiments assume no interference between units. Social feeds, shared workspaces, pricing, and marketplace systems violate this when treated users affect controls. Cluster randomization, geographic holdouts, or explicit network models may be required.
Principal-level reasoning
items: Map channels through which treatment can spill across units.
Choose the smallest randomization cluster that contains material interference.

contentBlocks.text: A larger sample cannot repair bias caused by untreated units receiving treatment indirectly.

Ignore spillovers because assignment itself remains random.

challenge.explanation: A larger sample cannot repair bias caused by untreated units receiving treatment indirectly.

lessons.title: Power, Minimum Detectable Effect, and Decision Value
lessons.summary: Size experiments around the smallest effect worth acting on, not a convenient sample.

contentBlocks.text: Power, Minimum Detectable Effect, and Decision Value

Power is the chance of detecting a real effect of a chosen size at a specified error rate. The minimum detectable effect should reflect product value and risk; underpowered tests waste users, while enormous tests can elevate trivial changes into statistically significant distractions.
Principal-level reasoning
items: Specify baseline variance and practical effect before launch.
Account for clustering, multiple metrics, and expected attrition.

contentBlocks.text: Statistical significance is not product significance; predefine what effect would change the decision.

lessons.summary: Stop exposure for clear harm without repeatedly peeking at the success metric.

contentBlocks.text: Implement a Sequential Safety Guardrail

Continuous monitoring inflates false positives when ordinary fixed-horizon thresholds are reused. A practical launch separates conservative always-on harm limits from a pre-registered success analysis, requiring minimum exposure before automatic rollback.

Return hold when samples are insufficient rather than declaring safety.

lessons.title: Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
lessons.summary: Find meaningful variation without turning subgroup search into storytelling.

contentBlocks.text: Heterogeneous Treatment Effects

Average effects can hide benefit for one population and harm for another. Subgroup analysis needs pre-specified slices or honest sample splitting, sufficient overlap, uncertainty intervals, and a policy explaining how heterogeneity changes treatment.
Principal-level reasoning
items: Distinguish discovery slices from confirmatory slices.
Check treatment propensity overlap within every reported group.

contentBlocks.text: A subgroup effect is actionable only when it is stable, supported, and tied to a deployment policy.

challenge.explanation: A subgroup effect is actionable only when it is stable, supported, and tied to a deployment policy.
hints: Distinguish discovery slices from confirmatory slices.

lessons.title: Causal Metric Architecture
lessons.summary: Preserve metric semantics and lineage across experimentation, analytics, and product reporting.

contentBlocks.text: Causal Metric Architecture

A causal metric is more than a SQL expression: it defines unit, eligibility, time window, censoring, attribution, missingness, and transformations. A versioned metric registry prevents teams from silently analyzing different outcomes under the same name.
Principal-level reasoning
items: Bind experiment analysis to immutable metric versions.
Record late-arriving data and window-completion policy.

lessons.summary: Use pre-treatment behavior to improve precision without leaking post-treatment information.

contentBlocks.text: Apply CUPED Variance Reduction

CUPED subtracts a scaled centered covariate correlated with the outcome. The covariate must be measured before treatment and computed consistently across arms; otherwise variance reduction can introduce bias.

lessons.title: Property Graphs, RDF, and Semantic Commitments
lessons.summary: Choose a graph model based on the meaning and interoperability the system must preserve.

contentBlocks.text: Property Graphs, RDF, and Semantic Commitments

Property graphs attach attributes to nodes and edges and fit traversal-heavy applications. RDF represents subject-predicate-object statements with global identifiers and optional ontologies. Neither format creates truth automatically; schemas and governance define what relationships mean.
Principal-level reasoning
items: Model relationship direction, cardinality, and validity explicitly.
Separate source assertions from inferred facts.

contentBlocks.text: A knowledge graph is a governed set of claims with identity and provenance, not a diagram of convenient links.

lessons.title: Entity Identity and Resolution
lessons.summary: Merge records only when evidence supports shared real-world identity.

contentBlocks.text: Entity Identity and Resolution

Entity resolution combines blocking, comparison features, scoring, and adjudication. False merges are often more damaging than missed links because they contaminate every downstream neighborhood, permission, and aggregate.
Principal-level reasoning

Calibrate merge thresholds by entity type and consequence.

lessons.title: Graph Storage and Query Architecture
lessons.summary: Match topology, consistency, and access patterns to an operational store.

contentBlocks.text: Graph Storage and Query Architecture

Native graph databases optimize traversals; relational tables can serve bounded graphs with mature transactions; RDF stores support semantic interoperability. The choice depends on query depth, mutation rate, consistency, tenant isolation, and operational expertise.
Principal-level reasoning
items: Benchmark representative path and update workloads.
Define tenant and row-level authorization before query execution.

contentBlocks.text: Choose a graph database for measured graph access patterns, not because the data can be drawn as nodes and edges.

lessons.title: Provenance for Graph Claims
lessons.summary: Track who asserted each edge, when, from which evidence, and under which transformation.

contentBlocks.text: Provenance for Graph Claims

A graph can combine authoritative records, extracted claims, and model inferences. Without claim-level provenance, downstream systems cannot distinguish a verified employment relationship from a low-confidence extraction or retract stale evidence.
Principal-level reasoning
items: Attach source, extraction version, confidence, and valid time.
Represent contradictory claims instead of overwriting them silently.

contentBlocks.text: Provenance turns an edge into an auditable claim rather than an unexplained fact.

lessons.title: Graph Embeddings and Structural Signals

contentBlocks.text: Graph Embeddings and Structural Signals

Graph embeddings compress neighborhood or relation patterns into vectors for similarity, classification, and link prediction. They can amplify degree bias, leak temporal information, and lose explicit paths, so production decisions should retain graph evidence and evaluate by structural slices.
Principal-level reasoning
items: Create train-test splits that respect graph time and connectivity.
Compare against simple degree and neighborhood baselines.

contentBlocks.text: An embedding score suggests a relationship; it does not establish that the relationship is true.

lessons.summary: Retrieve bounded paths only through authorized nodes and edges.

Graph RAG can expose private information through intermediate paths even when final nodes appear public. Authorization predicates must be applied during traversal, with depth, fan-out, and evidence budgets enforced before context reaches the model.

lessons.title: Temporal Graph Semantics
lessons.summary: Distinguish when a claim was true from when the system learned it.

contentBlocks.text: Temporal Graph Semantics

Valid time describes the real-world interval of a fact; transaction time describes when the database stored it. Bitemporal modeling supports corrected history, reproducible past queries, and audits that explain what the system believed at any moment.
Principal-level reasoning
items: Never overwrite history needed for prior-decision reconstruction.
Define interval boundaries and open-ended validity consistently.

lessons.title: Hybrid Graph and Vector Retrieval
lessons.summary: Route graph traversal and semantic search according to the question's evidence shape.

contentBlocks.text: Hybrid Graph and Vector Retrieval

Vector search finds conceptually similar text; graph traversal follows known typed relationships. A hybrid planner can retrieve semantic seeds, expand governed paths, rerank evidence, and expose exactly which step supplied each claim.
Principal-level reasoning
items: Set independent budgets for vector candidates and graph expansion.
Deduplicate evidence while preserving all contributing paths.

contentBlocks.text: Hybrid retrieval is strongest when each mechanism has a clear role and its failures remain observable.

Production graphs contain cycles, hubs, and malformed relationships. Path search needs depth and expansion limits, per-path visited sets, and deterministic ordering so one dense node cannot exhaust memory or produce unstable evidence.

Stop after both depth and result budgets are reached.

lessons.title: Privacy Threat Models for AI
lessons.summary: Define which attacker, auxiliary information, and disclosure the system must resist.

contentBlocks.text: Privacy Threat Models for AI

Privacy is not equivalent to removing names. Training examples can be memorized, embeddings can reveal membership, prompts can leak through traces, and outputs can combine innocuous facts into sensitive inference. A useful threat model names adversary access, protected unit, and unacceptable inference.
Principal-level reasoning
items: Distinguish record, user, household, and organization privacy units.
Trace sensitive data through training, retrieval, caching, telemetry, and support access.

contentBlocks.text: A privacy control is meaningful only relative to a stated adversary and protected information.

lessons.title: Differential Privacy Intuition
lessons.summary: Understand a guarantee that bounds how much one protected unit can influence output.

contentBlocks.text: Differential Privacy Intuition

Differential privacy compares output distributions on neighboring datasets that differ by one privacy unit. Epsilon measures distinguishability and delta allows a small failure probability; clipping bounds contribution and noise obscures it. The guarantee composes across repeated releases.
Principal-level reasoning
items: Choose the neighboring-dataset definition from the real privacy unit.
Track every mechanism that consumes the shared privacy budget.

lessons.title: Privacy Architecture Across the AI Lifecycle
lessons.summary: Enforce purpose, access, retention, and deletion across raw data and derivatives.

contentBlocks.text: Privacy Architecture Across the AI Lifecycle

A privacy-aware platform inventories source records, training datasets, embeddings, caches, prompts, traces, and model artifacts. It propagates purpose and retention metadata, restricts administrative access, and maintains lineage so deletion can reach derived assets.
Principal-level reasoning

Attach dataset and index lineage to every deployed model or retriever.

K-anonymity makes each quasi-identifier combination appear at least k times, but homogeneous groups can reveal a sensitive attribute and outside information can relink records. It can be a release heuristic, not a universal defense against inference.

contentBlocks.text: Federated Learning Boundaries

Federated learning aggregates client updates instead of centralizing raw examples. Updates can still leak information, malicious clients can poison training, and device availability biases participation. Secure aggregation, clipping, differential privacy, attestation, and robust aggregation address distinct risks.

contentBlocks.text: Machine Unlearning and Deletion Claims

Retraining without deleted data offers the clearest baseline but may be costly. Sharded training, adapter isolation, and certified removal can reduce cost; heuristic fine-tuning is not proof that influence vanished. Claims must match the method and evaluation.

lessons.title: Private Retrieval and Tenant Isolation
lessons.summary: Prevent unauthorized evidence from entering candidate generation, ranking, context, or telemetry.

contentBlocks.text: Private Retrieval and Tenant Isolation

RAG crosses identity, vector indexing, document ACLs, model context, cache, and trace boundaries. Tenant and document filters must apply before similarity search or graph expansion where possible, with per-tenant encryption, namespaces, and cache keys.
Principal-level reasoning

contentBlocks.text: Implement a Deterministic Attack Mutator

Mutation pipelines can explode combinatorially. Generate stable IDs from source and operator sequence, deduplicate identical outputs, and cap per-source expansion so evaluation remains reproducible and affordable.

contentBlocks.text:
def build_variants(source,operators,limit=20):
    import hashlib
    seen=set(); variants=[]
    for op in operators:
        text=op["apply"](source["text"])
        if text in seen: continue
        seen.add(text)
        case_id=hashlib.sha256((source["id"]+"|"+op["id"]+"|"+text).encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
        variants.append({"id":case_id,"source_id":source["id"],
                         "operators":[op["id"]],"text":text})
        if len(variants)>=limit: break
    return variants
